description: Join our team to tackle the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge! We're building an interactive Space Mission Design Game that turns complex space engineering into an engaging, gamified simulator. Bring your passion for coding, vision systems, or web design to craft an impressive prototype and win together!
summary: Orbit & Outplay: Exoplanet Survey is a turn-based mission-design roguelite built in Godot 4.7 and playable in the browser. You have $500M, a fragile approval rating and three missions to survive. Design a survey craft under budget and fairing mass, then draft one of 72 real exoplanets from the NASA Exoplanet Archive and fly a telegraphed hazard course across its surface. Every number comes from archive data: equilibrium temperature sets heat load, mass and radius set surface gravity and delta-v cost, distance sets downlink loss, and stellar type shapes the radiation environment. A Mission Architecture Review commits each run with a transfer arc, the four NASA mission segments and a launch-to-end ConOps timeline; debriefs convert results into science points, grants and refits; the campaign ends in an agency grade from C to S. The goal is to make the tension of coupled mission trade-offs something a player can feel and explain.
details:
Orbit & Outplay is a turn-based tactical systems-engineering roguelite. It answers the challenge brief "Space Mission Design Game" by turning the coupled trade-offs of real mission design into something a player can feel turn by turn.

What it does. A run has three phases. (1) Mission design: choose a hull, a launch vehicle, a science objective and two instruments under a hard $500M budget and the launcher's fairing mass. Six live bars — mass, power, delta-v, hull integrity, thermal margin, data capacity — update immediately, and validation blocks an over-budget or over-mass stack. (2) Target draft: three real exoplanets are drawn from the NASA Exoplanet Archive, each with measured equilibrium temperature, surface gravity, distance, host star and biome, plus the derived hazard bars the mission will face. (3) Surface sector: a chunked pixel-art alien surface where each turn allows one move within a 3–4 tile range. Selecting a destination previews the path, delta-v/sol cost, heat load and whether the route crosses a hazard. Hazards are telegraphed one turn ahead and resolve at the end of the turn — stellar flares, thermal surges, dust storms, quakes, radiation belts, eclipse shadows, cryogenic cold, superflares, tidal shocks, ion storms. Blockable hazards can be absorbed with power; HOLD vents heat and recharges; EXTRACT banks data. Collect the quota and leave, or push for the fourth node and the full-sweep grant.

Between sectors a Mission Architecture Review commits the mission with a transfer arc, the four NASA mission segments, CML and a launch-to-end ConOps timeline. Debriefs convert results into science points, a grant and an approval change, then offer refit modules and a seeded agency event with two trade-offs. Every second sector switches to RELAY SURVEY, planting three beacons. Three sectors produce an agency ledger with a grade from C to S.

NASA data as a mechanic. The 72-planet pool is curated from the Exoplanet Archive's Planetary Systems Composite Parameters (pscomppars) table. Equilibrium temperature drives thermal load and starting heat; mass and radius drive surface gravity and delta-v cost; stellar age, spectral type and insolation drive the radiation environment; distance drives communications loss. Missing or physically implausible archive masses use the Chen & Kipping (2017) mass–radius relation and are flagged as estimates. The raw archive snapshot, the build script and the formula table are in the repository, so every derived value is reproducible.

Impact. Mission design is normally taught with static forms, which teach vocabulary but not tension. A student who plays one sector can explain a failure: the telemetry was visible, the hazard was telegraphed, the route was a choice. That explainability is the point.

Tools. Godot 4.7.2 (GDScript) with a WebGL2 browser export; Python for the data pipeline (archive parsing, mission formulas, validation), asset generation and QA automation; Playwright for end-to-end browser testing; ComfyUI (SDXL + Pixel Art XL) for art assets; Git and GitHub for version control.

Creativity and constraints. A single static, install-free browser build at 640×360 pixel resolution; honest abstraction documented rather than hidden (Chen–Kipping estimates flagged, Hohmann-style transfer simplified and labelled); 1–4 player hot-seat crew mode with per-role goals and a shared campaign code; no online accounts, no server.
